label: Yehezkel (Ezekiel) — Part 4 — Chapters 25–32
summary_plain: YHWH delivers oracles against the nations: Ammon, Moav, Edom, the Pelishtim. Then Tyre — the great maritime trading city. The prince of Tyre says: I am a god, I sit in the seat of gods in the heart of the seas. YHWH responds: You are a man and not a god. A lamentation over the king of Tyre: You were in Eden, the garden of The Creator. You were the anointed guardian kerub. You were blameless from the day you were created until unrighteousness was found in you. Against Mitsrayim: Pharaoh the great dragon lying in his rivers. YHWH will scatter Mitsrayim among the nations. The Assyrian was a cedar in Lebanon — great and tall — yet he was brought down to Sheol. Pharaoh shall be laid among the uncircumcised in the pit.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from the DSS Ezekiel fragments and the Orit Ge'ez. The Tyre oracles (chapters 26-28) are among the most significant in the prophetic literature. Chapter 28:12-19 — the lamentation over the king of Tyre — describes a figure in Eden, adorned with precious stones, the anointed guardian kerub who walked among the stones of fire until violence was found in him. This passage, alongside Yesha'yahu 14, forms the primary Hebrew prophetic material later systematized into the 'fall of Satan' narrative — though the original text describes the king of Tyre, not a supernatural being. The Mitsrayim oracles (chapters 29-32) include the cedar of Lebanon parable (chapter 31) and the descent to Sheol (chapter 32) — an underworld geography describing where fallen powers are laid.

key_terms.definition: YHWH declares judgment against Ammon for saying Aha! over the defilement of the Temple and the desolation of Yisra'el. Ammon will be given over to the people of the east; their cities will become pasture for camels. They will know that YHWH is YHWH.

Three chapters dedicated to Tyre, the great Phoenician maritime trading city. Tyre said Aha! over Yerushalayim's fall: the gate of the peoples is broken; it has swung open to me. YHWH will bring Nebukhadnetzar against Tyre, destroying its walls and towers, scraping it bare like a rock, burying it in the sea. You shall be no more.

key_terms.term: Lament Over the Prince of Tyre (Ezekiel 28:1-19)
key_terms.definition: The prince of Tyre said he was a god, sitting in the seat of gods in the heart of the seas. YHWH declares he will bring strangers against him. The lament extends to a covering cherub in the garden of Eden, full of wisdom and beauty, profaned by his own sin, cast down from the mountain of YHWH.

key_terms.term: You Were the Signet of Perfection (Ezekiel 28:12-19)
key_terms.definition: YHWH's dirge over the king of Tyre uses imagery of the garden of Eden: You were the signet of perfection, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty. You were in Eden, the garden of YHWH; every precious stone was your covering. He was a guardian cherub on YHWH's holy mountain. But his heart became proud because of his beauty and he was cast to the ground.

key_terms.term: Oracle Against Mitzrayim — Pharaoh the Great Dragon (Ezekiel 29)
key_terms.definition: YHWH's oracle against Pharaoh king of Mitzrayim: Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lies in the midst of his streams. YHWH will put hooks in his jaws and drag him out of the Nile. Mitzrayim will be a staff of reed to Yisra'el — it always broke when leaned upon.

A funeral lament over Pharaoh: You consider yourself a lion of the nations, but you are like a dragon in the seas. YHWH will drag Pharaoh out and cast his flesh on the mountains, covering the heavens and causing the sun, moon, and stars to go dark. Pharaoh will descend to Sheol among the slain.

key_terms.term: Nations Knowing That I Am YHWH
key_terms.definition: Throughout Ezekiel 25-32, every oracle against the nations ends with the same refrain: then they shall know that I am YHWH. The judgment of Ammon, Moav, Edom, Philistia, Tyre, Sidon, and Mitzrayim all serve the same covenant purpose: demonstrating YHWH's sovereignty over all nations, not just Yisra'el.

YHWH declares judgment against Sidon, Tyre's northern neighbor: pestilence and blood in her streets. After this YHWH will gather Yisra'el from the peoples among whom they are scattered, and they will dwell securely in their land. The judgment of nations is paired with the promise of Yisra'el's restoration.

Moav said the house of Judah is like all the other nations, denying Yisra'el's covenant distinctiveness. Edom took revenge on the house of Yehudah. Both will be judged: Moav exposed to the people of the east, Edom cut off. Edom's judgment is particularly severe because of family betrayal — Edom is descended from Esav, Ya'aqov's brother.

key_terms.term: Cedar of Lebanon Metaphor for Mitzrayim (Ezekiel 31)
key_terms.definition: YHWH asks Pharaoh: Consider Ashur, a cedar of Lebanon, beautiful in its branches, with its top among the clouds. All the birds nested in it, all the beasts gave birth under it. But it became proud because of its height, and YHWH gave it over to be cut down. Pharaoh is told: you shall be brought down with the trees of Eden to the depths of the earth.

faq.question: What is the theological purpose of the oracles against nations in Ezekiel 25-32?
faq.answer: The oracles against Ammon, Moav, Edom, Philistia, Tyre, Sidon, and Mitzrayim serve a single covenant purpose: demonstrating that YHWH's sovereignty extends over all nations, not just Yisra'el. Each oracle ends with then they shall know that I am YHWH. These nations thought YHWH's judgment on Yisra'el meant YHWH was weak or defeated. The oracles declare the opposite: YHWH used Babylon as his instrument of judgment on Yisra'el; YHWH will also judge Babylon's allies and opponents in turn. No nation is outside YHWH's covenant governance.

faq.question: Why does Tyre receive three chapters of judgment in Ezekiel 26-28?
faq.answer: Tyre receives the most extended judgment of any nation in Ezekiel because of the nature of its sin: when Yerushalayim fell, Tyre said the gate of the peoples is broken — it has swung open to me. Tyre saw Yerushalayim's destruction as a commercial opportunity. This celebration of a covenant community's destruction, combined with Tyre's commercial pride and its prince's claim to divinity, made it a paradigmatic case of the hubris YHWH judges.

faq.question: What is the Eden imagery in Ezekiel 28:12-19 about?
faq.answer: The lament over the king of Tyre uses Eden imagery to describe his original state and his fall: you were the signet of perfection, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in Eden, the garden of YHWH. He was a guardian cherub on YHWH's holy mountain, blameless, until iniquity was found in him. His heart became proud because of his beauty. This is YHWH's indictment of pride: the most beautifully gifted creature, given the highest position, fell because beauty became self-worship rather than service to the Creator.

faq.question: Why does YHWH call Pharaoh the great dragon in Ezekiel 29?
faq.answer: YHWH's description of Pharaoh as the great dragon that lies in the midst of his streams deliberately echoes the creation narrative and the exodus tradition. The Nile was Mitzrayim's source of life and power; Pharaoh who controlled it claimed divine ownership of the waters. Pharaoh's claim that the Nile was his own is the paradigmatic form of creature claiming creator status. YHWH will put hooks in his jaws and drag him out.

faq.question: What does the staff of reed metaphor say about Mitzrayim as an ally?
faq.answer: In Ezekiel 29:6-7, YHWH says Mitzrayim has been a staff of reed to the house of Yisra'el: when the hand grasped it, it broke and pierced the shoulder; when leaned upon, it splintered. This was the historical reality of Yisra'el's diplomatic relationship with Mitzrayim: every time Judah turned to Mitzrayim for military support against Assyria or Babylon, Mitzrayim failed to deliver, most catastrophically when Pharaoh's army turned back and left Yerushalayim to fall to Nebukhadnetzar.

faq.question: What is Edom's specific judgment and why is it more severe than others?
faq.answer: In Ezekiel 25:12-14, Edom's judgment is delivered through the hand of YHWH's own people, not through foreign nations like the others. Edom, descended from Esav, took revenge on the house of Yehudah. Family betrayal is the aggravating factor: when Yerushalayim fell to Babylon, Edom participated in or celebrated the destruction of their covenant kin. Covenant kinship betrayal carries the heaviest judgment in the prophetic tradition.

faq.question: How does the fall of the proud cedar in Ezekiel 31 warn Pharaoh?
faq.answer: In Ezekiel 31, YHWH uses Ashur, formerly the world's greatest empire, as the cedar of Lebanon: once beautiful, with top among the clouds, all nations sheltering in its branches. But it became proud because of its height, and YHWH gave it over to be cut down. The warning to Pharaoh is explicit: you shall be brought down with the trees of Eden. Greatness divorced from YHWH's governance ends in Sheol — the same fate has come for every empire that became too proud.

faq.question: Why does Ezekiel 32 describe Pharaoh's descent into Sheol?
faq.answer: In Ezekiel 32, YHWH gives a full funeral dirge over Pharaoh: descending into Sheol, he will be met by all the other fallen empires — Ashur, Elam, Edom — all lying among the uncircumcised, killed by the sword. This scene of Sheol as the great equalizer makes the point: Mitzrayim's pride as the oldest and greatest civilization ends in the same place as every other empire that defied YHWH. The mighty Pharaoh will lie with the uncircumcised in Sheol — the ultimate reversal of royal glory.

faq.question: What does the judgment of nations reveal about YHWH's covenant governance?
faq.answer: The oracles against nations in Ezekiel 25-32 reveal that YHWH's covenant governance is universal, not tribal. YHWH does not judge only covenant-violating Yisra'el but every nation according to universal moral standards: gloating over others' disasters (Ammon, Moav), family betrayal (Edom), commercial exploitation (Tyre), claiming divine self-sufficiency (Pharaoh). These standards are not specifically Hebrew covenant law but universal ethical standards embedded in creation itself. YHWH is Creator of all nations, and all nations are accountable to him.

faq.question: What is the significance of Sidon's oracle being paired with the promise of Yisra'el's restoration?
faq.answer: In Ezekiel 28:20-26, the oracle against Sidon is immediately followed by YHWH's promise to gather Yisra'el from the peoples and restore them to their land: they shall dwell securely, and no one shall make them afraid. The pairing is deliberate: YHWH's judgment of the surrounding nations clears the hostile environment for Yisra'el's restoration. The scattered people cannot return to a land surrounded by enemies who celebrate their destruction. The oracles against nations are covenant preparation, clearing the way for YHWH to restore his covenant people to their land.

faq.question: What does the Eden/Tyre oracle reveal about pride and covenant?
faq.answer: Yehezkel 28 uses Eden imagery to expose the king of Tyre's pride: 'You were in Eden, the garden of YHWH... perfect in your ways from the day you were created, till unrighteousness was found in you.' The oracle draws directly on covenant memory of Eden — the place of YHWH's presence, abundance, and beauty — and applies it to Tyre's self-exaltation. The king of Tyre saw himself as perfect and permanent, beyond accountability. YHWH's verdict is that pride in one's own beauty and wisdom is the original covenant breach. The same pattern that began in Eden — a creature claiming divine status — produces the same judgment: expulsion, destruction, being brought to the dust.
